refnamediv.refpurpose: smooth 2D plot of a surface defined by a function using colors

refsynopsisdiv.title: Syntax
refsynopsisdiv.synopsis: Sfgrayplot(x, y, f, <opt_args>) Sfgrayplot(x, y, f [,strf, rect, nax, zminmax, colminmax, mesh, colout]) h = Sfgrayplot(...)

listitem.para: Real matrices defining the grid : x and y can be row vectors of sizes n1 and n2 or matrices of the same size (n1,n2) (curvilinear grid).
a Scilab function of two variables.
Rectangular grid: f is called as z(i,j) = f(x(i), y(j)) via feval(x, y, f); it receives scalar arguments and must return a scalar.

Non-rectangular grid: f is called as Z = f(X, Y) where X and Y are full matrices; it must return a matrix of the same size (n, m). The function should therefore be vectorized, using element-wise operators (.*, ./, .^, etc.).

this represents a sequence of statements key1=value1, key2=value2, ... where key1, key2, ... can be one of the following: strf, rect, nax, zminmax, colminmax, mesh, colout (see plot2d for the first three and fec for the last four).
Optional output handle to the created Fec entity. For a list of properties, see fec_properties.

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: Sfgrayplot is the same as fgrayplot but the plot is smoothed. The function fec is used for smoothing. The surface is plotted assuming that it is linear on a set of triangles built from the grid (here with n1=5, n2=3):

listitem.para: Rectangular grid: Sfgrayplot(x, y, f) where x and y are vectors. The function f is evaluated on the full Cartesian product of x and y using feval(x, y, f), so f receives scalar arguments.

Non-rectangular (curvilinear) grid: Sfgrayplot(X, Y, f) where X and Y are matrices of the same size (n, m). The function is evaluated as Z = f(X, Y), so f must be vectorized (accepting and returning matrices). This form is selected automatically when at least one of the first two arguments has more than one row and more than one column.

refsection.para: In both modes the grid is triangulated the same way: each quad (i,j)-(i+1,j)-(i,j+1)-(i+1,j+1) is split into two triangles along the diagonal, and fec interpolates the computed Z values linearly inside each triangle.
The function colorbar may be used to see the color scale (but you must know or compute the min and max values of the surface).
Instead of Sfgrayplot, you can use Sgrayplot when the Z values are already available, and this may be slightly faster.
Enter the command Sfgrayplot() to see a demo.

refsection.title: Examples
refsection.programlisting: // example #1: rectangular grid — plot 4 surfaces function z=surf1(x,y), z=x*y, endfunction function z=surf2(x,y), z=x^2-y^2, endfunction function z=surf3(x,y), z=x^3+y^2, endfunction function z=surf4(x,y), z=x^2+y^2, endfunction clf() set(gcf(),"color_map",[jet(64);hot(64)]) x = linspace(-1,1,60); y = linspace(-1,1,60); drawlater(); subplot(2,2,1) colorbar(-1,1,[1,64]) Sfgrayplot(x,y,surf1,strf="041",colminmax=[1,64]) xtitle("f(x,y) = x*y") subplot(2,2,2) colorbar(-1,1,[65,128]) Sfgrayplot(x,y,surf2,strf="041",colminmax=[65,128]) xtitle("f(x,y) = x^2-y^2") subplot(2,2,3) colorbar(-1,2,[65,128]) Sfgrayplot(x,y,surf3,strf="041",colminmax=[65,128]) xtitle("f(x,y) = x^3+y^2") subplot(2,2,4) colorbar(0,2,[1,64]) Sfgrayplot(x,y,surf4,strf="041",colminmax=[1,64]) xtitle("f(x,y) = x^2+y^2") drawnow(); show_window()

revision.revremark: Non-rectangular (curvilinear) grid support: X,Y,Z can now be matrices of the same size.
